newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran supreme leader rejects talking with U.S..
newsitem.headline: Iran supreme leader rejects talking with U.S..

text.p: Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on Wednesday rejected suggestions that talks could be held with Washington, saying it was only a tactic by the United States to undermine opposing states.

In a speech marking the 1979 seizure of the United States embassy in Tehran by Moslem militants, Khamenei said Washington tried to defeat its opponents first by exerting political and economic pressure on them and then proposing talks.
He said such talks would undermine a government's popularity at home and its respect around the world.
"The American politicians' mistake was to use this method against a powerful and self-reliant entity such as the Iranian nation," Khamenei said in the speech broadcast on Tehran radio.

Khamenei was apparently referring to remarks by U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Pelletreau who said during a visit to the region last week that Washington would like to hold talks with Iran on bilateral differences.

"Even if there were 10 powers such as America in the world confronting such a nation (Iran), they could not bring any harm to this nation," Khamenei told a gathering of students. They responded by chanting "Death to America" and the Moslem rallying cry of "Allahu Akbar" (God is Greatest).
Iran's anti-U.S. stance did not mean Tehran would seek or provoke a military confrontation with Washington, but it would strongly respond to any U.S. aggression, Khamenei said.
"Where we can in the world we will expose injustices perpetrated by America. And everywhere, we will be on the side of those oppressed by (U.S.) arrogance," Khamenei added.
The United States broke diplomatic ties with Iran in 1980 after the embassy seizure in which 52 Americans were held hostage for 444 days.

The United States imposed a trade and investment ban on Iran in June 1995, accusing it of sponsoring terrorism and seeking to develop nuclear weapons. Iran denies the charges and says the United States is bent on destroying the Islamic government.
A U.S. law in effect since August tightened the sanctions to include non-U.S. firms.
